About this citation

There is no single canonical numbering. The Brunschvicg (1897) and Lafuma (1951) systems differ, and a fragment number is meaningless without saying which it follows — a point the corpus flags where it records 'common numbering'. Pascal died before arranging the material, so the order of the fragments is editorial throughout.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.”

French

“Le cœur a ses raisons que la raison ne connaît point.”

The archive cites the Brunschvicg numbering. The Pensées are numbered differently in the Lafuma and Sellier editions, so the section number will not match a source that uses a different scheme — a real hazard for anyone trying to check the line.

### Attribution notes

The French is usually mistranslated as “the heart has reasons that reason cannot know,” which makes it a rejection of reason. The French says reason does not know them, not that they are unknowable — the heart's reasons are ones the discursive intellect has not reached. Pascal's target is the theology of his own century, not reason as such.

#### About Blaise Pascal

Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, and Christian apologist who invented an early calculator and advanced probability and fluid mechanics. After a decisive religious conversion, he defended Jansenism in the Provincial Letters and left unfinished Pensées.

### How to read this passage

Aesthetics asks what beauty is, how taste is educated, and how art discloses truth or shapes moral perception. This passage enters that discussion through beauty, reason.
